title: How can you tell if something was written by ChatGPT? (Washington Post analysis via Boston Globe)
tell: Measured on shared gpt-4o chats to July 2025: emoji in ~70% of messages (green-check emoji 11x human rate); em dash in more than half of responses (under 1 in 10 a year earlier); 'not just X but Y' in ~6% of chats; 'core' 5x, 'modern' in 8%; contractions rose (you're/it's in ~1/3 of chats). 'Delve' fell to ~1 in 1000 and 'ensure/crucial/significant' fell: tells drift with model version, so a word list ages. Clusters, not single tells, are the signal.
example: emoji-led bullets; 'It's not just X, it's Y'; em dashes in most replies
fix: Do not copy a static banned list; re-check against current output. No emoji or em dash in casual messages unless the person really writes that way; commas, periods, plain contractions.

title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing (WP:COLLABCOMM, AIBOLD, AILIST, AIEMOJI, MARKDOWN)
tell: Chatbot correspondence pasted into a post: words to watch 'I hope this helps', 'Of course!', 'Certainly!', 'You're absolutely right!', 'Here's a template for...'. Also: boldface on every instance of a key phrase ('key takeaways' style); lists whose markers are followed by an inline bold header; emoji before headings/bullets; markdown syntax (headers, **bold**, '>' quotes) in plain-text venues, though Markdown alone is weak evidence; answer-style preambles ('Answer: Here are several...'); hedging disclaimers; subtly positive/promotional tone; 'It's important to recognize that...' moralising.
example: 'Here's a template for your wiki user page. You can copy and paste this onto your user page and customize it further.' / '🌍 My Mission: To support the sharing of free, accurate, and reliable information' / 'A **leveraged buyout (LBO)** is characterized by the extensive use of **debt financing**' / 'Conflict of Interest (COI)/Autobiography: While I understand the concern...'
fix: Start with the content, no greeting, offer or sign-off; plain text in chat/forum venues; bold at most one thing; no emoji bullets; prose paragraphs instead of bold-header lists.

title: Are Em Dashes Really a Sign of AI Writing? (Rolling Stone; seen via search snippet, fetch redirected)
tell: Ordinary readers lean hard on the em dash: a r/ChatGPT post said a colleague's emails seemed AI-written because of frequent em dashes; the 'ChatGPT hyphen' went viral. Skeptics note humans use it too, so it convicts only in volume and in venues where the person never used one.
example: colleague's emails 'full of em dashes' read as AI
fix: Replace dashes with a period or comma; one in a long piece at most (the Writing-Bible list suggests ~1 per 500 words).

title: TechRadar: the em dash giveaway is over (snippet only; page body not retrieved)
tell: Per the search summary it quotes a Reddit user saying the main giveaway is that the writing emphasises everything (uniform intensity, nothing is ranked). Body not read, so treat as a lead.
fix: Let some points be flat and brief; spend emphasis on one thing.

title: Paul Graham: AI-written founder emails feel like being lied to
tell: A reader who spots AI authorship stops reading and trusts the sender less, assuming they cannot write or are deceiving; the cue Graham names is a 'hard-hitting journalistic style' in cold emails. Cost of detection is trust, not just style.
example: 'like being lied to'; he will not finish reading such emails
fix: Write the email yourself in your own plain voice; a rough true note beats a polished generic one.

title: Paul Graham: Writing, Briefly / Write Simply
tell: Fancy words and complex sentences make the reader do extra work 'just so you can seem cool'; simple writing exposes empty thinking: 'If you say nothing simply, it will be obvious to everyone, including you.' (This is the mechanism behind slop: polish with nothing under it.)
example: 'I try to write using ordinary words and simple sentences.' / 'Much of this editing is cutting'
fix: Ordinary words, simple sentences, fast first draft then days of cutting; complexity only on purpose.

title: Mark Brinker: Using AI to Write Website Copy? Watch This First
tell: AI slop copy is polished but interchangeable: could describe almost any business, no position, no objections answered, no next step. Cause: a vague prompt and first-draft acceptance.
example: 'We provide innovative solutions.' / 'Take your business to the next level.' / 'Unlock your full potential.'
fix: Supply real notes, client questions, examples; decide the page's job (answer a question, address a concern, prevent a mistake) before drafting; outline, then one section at a time; check each reads like something you would say.

title: Kalungi: prompt AI for better marketing copy (snippet)
tell: Default AI marketing vocabulary people do not say aloud: 'leverage', 'seamless', 'robust', 'elevate'. Without a sample of the brand's voice the model falls back on a polished, generic default. Vendor blog; weak evidence.
fix: Give it a real voice sample and ask for plainer words; better, write from customer language.

title: Marketing Copywriting Cliches to Avoid (snippet)
tell: Pre-AI evidence that the promise-verb cluster is old marketing cliche, not new: 'elevate', 'streamline', 'propel', 'accelerate', 'skyrocket your business to the next level', 'maximize your profits'. LLMs inherit it from human marketing.
example: 'skyrocket your business to the next level'
fix: State the concrete result (what changes, by how much, for whom) instead of a verb of ascent.

title: CXL: Use Voice-of-Customer Research to Boost Conversions (snippet; Joanna Wiebe / Copyhackers method)
tell: Good copywriters do not invent phrasing: they mine reviews, surveys, interviews and comments, highlight repeated words, and reuse them. Reported (secondary) case: a rehab-centre headline lifted from a book review got 400%+ more clicks. Wiebe's Seven Sweeps include clarity, 'so what', 'prove it', specificity.
example: headline swiped from a customer's own review
fix: Collect real customer wording first; run 'so what?' and 'prove it' passes on every claim; keep the rough human phrasing when it carries the punch.

title: Jason Fried (37signals): Then just say it like that
tell: Written homepage copy dressed up 'because marketing' fell flat; the plain spoken version was better than anything he had written. The AI-copy version of this is the dressed-up register.
example: 'They were better than anything I'd written' / 'I tried doctoring them up a bit because "marketing" ... and, once again, they fell flat.'
fix: Say the point aloud, write down what you said, and do not doctor it.

title: AI & What I'm Noticing As An Agency Owner (snippet only; fetch 404)
tell: Per search summary: polite-but-bland cadence, stock descriptors like 'modern elegance' and 'timeless sophistication', em dashes. Body not read.
fix: Name the actual thing (material, price, who it is for) instead of a mood adjective.

title: Computational Turing Test (Nov 2025; X, Bluesky, Reddit; nine open-weight models)
tell: Classifiers separate LLM replies from human replies at roughly 70-80% (search summary figure; abstract says 'clearly distinguishable even after calibration'). Largest gaps: affective tone and emotional expression (toxicity, sentiment). Instruction-tuned models were MORE detectable than base models; bigger models were not more human. Human-likeness trades off against semantic fidelity. Style examples and retrieved context helped (summary, not confirmed in abstract).
fix: Humans on social platforms are blunter, more negative, more emotionally uneven than assistant-tuned text; do not default to even, agreeable, balanced tone; ground replies in the thread's specifics.

title: Under the Surface: Tracking the Artifactuality of LLM-Generated Data (snippet; 110 paired posts, qualitative)
tell: Per search summary: human posts use deliberate non-standard grammar, punctuation, capitalisation and spelling to carry tone; 52% of machine texts used full punctuation where the paired human text did not; machine text had more intensifiers, adjectives and emoji; 21% of machine texts lacked discourse markers the human had. Small qualitative sample; figures are from a secondary summary.
example: human: 'lol no. not even close' / machine: 'That's a great point, and not even close in my view.'
fix: Allow fragments, lowercase, dropped periods and discourse markers (well, honestly, anyway) in casual registers; match the venue's own mechanics.

title: Linguistic analysis of human vs LLM comments on Brazilian Reddit communities (snippet)
tell: LLM comments align well with post content and style and are more informative, but are repetitive and harder to read; human comments are shorter, more varied and contain personal experience.
fix: Shorter; one concrete personal detail or anecdote; vary shape comment to comment.

title: Hacker News Guidelines
tell: Policy: 'Don't post generated comments or AI-edited comments.' HN is for conversation between humans (dang: 'We don't allow genai text on HN itself'; enforcement is by flags, not a detector). Confirms communities treat even AI-edited text as unwelcome.
fix: In a venue like this, text must be the person's own; a light-touch edit still counts.

title: Stack Overflow moderators strike over AI policy (snippet; stackoverflow.com fetch refused by tool)
tell: SO banned ChatGPT answers in Dec 2022, then in 2023 told moderators to stop removing posts merely for suspected AI use because detectors give false positives; moderators struck. Mod detection leaned on flags and judgement, not tools. Current (2026) policy not verified; stackoverflow.com could not be fetched.
fix: Detection is unreliable, so do not rely on passing a detector; the real defence is specific, correct, first-hand content.

title: Adobe Express report on AI-written email trust (snippet; vendor survey)
tell: Vendor survey: 30% of consumers not confident they can tell AI from human email; 18% say they unsubscribed from a marketing email because they suspected AI. Georgia Tech CHI 2022 (nlp.stanford.edu/~diyiy/docs/chi22_perception.pdf): trust in the writer fell when told AI was involved, reversed for more interpersonal emails. Ohio State / Florida studies (secondary news): AI-written messages read as lazy, insincere, esp. congratulations/motivation from managers.
fix: For personal or relational messages especially, write it yourself; generic and impersonal reads as low effort.

title: Leftover scaffolding as the cheapest giveaway (Boston Globe + search summaries)
tell: Unfilled placeholders ('[Name]'), 'As a large language model...', and generic impersonal/repetitive emails are the tells ordinary readers actually catch with certainty.
fix: Check for brackets and meta-talk before sending; add one detail only the sender would know.
